analysis.one_liner: Exempts most over-the-counter derivatives and swaps from federal regulation.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on this bill, but its substance became law that December, freeing swaps and energy derivatives from federal oversight.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Commodity Exchange Act to strip most over-the-counter derivatives — including swaps and energy contracts traded between big financial players — out from under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's rules. It would leave those private deals largely unregulated while keeping basic oversight of traditional futures exchanges. Supporters said this gave banks legal certainty and kept derivatives trading from moving overseas.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks, investment houses, energy traders, and other 'eligible contract participants' — institutions with more than $10 million in assets — would gain a legal green light to write and trade swap agreements and other derivatives without registering the contracts, reporting them, or worrying that courts might void them. Exchanges also gain new flexibility to run electronic trading platforms and lighter-touch registration as derivatives execution facilities.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that federal law gives neither the SEC nor the CFTC jurisdiction over swap agreements, removing the legal uncertainty that had clouded the market.

Excludes transactions in financial commodities (interest rates, currencies, credit risk) and energy commodities from the Commodity Exchange Act when made between 'eligible contract participants' off organized exchanges.
Excludes foreign currency, government securities, security warrants, repurchase transactions, and mortgage or mortgage-purchase contracts from coverage under the Act.

Lets boards of trade elect lighter registration as derivatives transaction execution facilities instead of full contract-market designation, and authorizes electronic trading facilities outside the Act.
States that contracts between eligible parties cannot be voided or made unenforceable just because they fall under an exemption, giving banks confidence their deals will hold up in court.
Authorizes appropriations for the CFTC through fiscal year 2005.

analysis.who_pays: If the framework had failed or blown up, the costs would land on ordinary people: pension savers and workers whose retirement funds, banks, and insurers sit behind these unregulated bets, and taxpayers who backstop failing financial institutions. Retail customers would also face less protection in retail foreign-currency deals except where limited CFTC jurisdiction is retained.

drawbacks.text: The exclusion of swaps and over-the-counter transactions in financial and energy commodities removes the main federal regulator from a market where large institutions trade bets on defaults, interest rates, and energy prices with little transparency — a structure later associated with the unregulated credit-default-swasp exposure that amplified the 2008 crisis and the 'Enron loophole' in energy trading.

The 'eligible contract participant' definition reaches any entity with over $10 million in assets managing business risk, and even commodity pools with $5 million in assets whose investors need not themselves qualify — so the exemption covers a broad, loosely defined universe of institutions rather than only sophisticated financial firms.

The bill requires the CFTC to weigh costs and benefits before issuing orders or rules, a shift that its critics could argue slows the regulator exactly when fast action matters; only emergency actions and investigations are excepted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The honest case for the bill was real: swaps contracts had sat in legal limbo for a decade, and banks argued that without legal certainty the market would migrate offshore, costing the US its edge in finance. But the cost side was enormous and largely hidden at the time. The bill carves the fastest-growing, riskiest corner of the financial system — bilateral swaps and energy derivatives — out of federal oversight entirely, with no public reporting, no capital rules, and no regulator watching for systemic buildup. History's verdict was harsh: the market this bill freed became the transmission channel through which the 2008 financial crisis spread from Wall Street to ordinary households' jobs, homes, and retirement accounts.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Agriculture Committee reported the bill favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar in August 2000, but the Senate never took it up before the 106th Congress ended — while the House moved an identical measure into law that December.

narrative.text: Introduced June 8, 2000 by Senator Lugar for himself, Senator Gramm, and Senator Fitzgerald, and read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The Agriculture Committee held joint hearings with the Senate Banking Committee on June 21, 2000.
The committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on June 29, 2000.

The committee reported the bill on August 25, 2000 with a substitute amendment and written report No. 106-390, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 766.
No further Senate action followed; the bill sat on the calendar until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, never reaching a floor vote.

The reported version excluded swaps, foreign currency, government securities, mortgage transactions, and over-the-counter transactions in financial and energy commodities from coverage under the Commodity Exchange Act, and stated that nothing in the Act gives the SEC or the CFTC jurisdiction over swap agreements.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's backers did not lose. Widely reported history: a House companion carrying the same deregulation passed and was signed into law in December 2000, so banks, derivatives dealers, and energy traders got what this bill promised, without the federal oversight it stripped away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and derivatives dealers, whose substance became law

for.name: Sen. Richard Lugar
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, held joint hearings, reported it favorably with a substitute amendment, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Sen. Phil Gramm
for.role: Senate Banking Committee chairman; named in the bill's introduction
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alongside Lugar; the deregulatory structure it embodied was the centerpiece of his banking-agenda work that Congress.

for.name: House leadership of the 106th Congress
for.role: Attached the companion Commodity Futures Modernization Act (H.R. 4541) to a year-end omnibus bill and passed it
for.what_they_did: Enacted the same derivative deregulation into law in December 2000 after the Senate bill stalled.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the companion Commodity Futures Modernization Act into law on December 21, 2000.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition appears in the Senate record: the Agriculture Committee reported the bill favorably without a roll-call vote, and the companion law passed Congress with overwhelming support from both parties and was signed by a Democratic president.

industries.industry: Wall Street banks and over-the-counter derivatives dealers
industries.note: The bill exempts their swap and OTC derivatives business from CFTC jurisdiction and makes those contracts legally enforceable with no federal oversight. Their gain in freedom from regulation came at the expense of the transparency and capital rules that would later have caught the buildup that spread the 2008 crisis to ordinary households.

Over-the-counter energy derivatives (crude oil, natural gas, electricity) fall under the exclusion for energy commodities between eligible contract participants, so electronic energy trading desks would operate free of the Act. This is the provision structure later called the 'Enron loophole.'

The bill creates a lighter registration path for derivatives transaction execution facilities, authorizes electronic trading, and registers derivatives clearing organizations — locking exchanges into the market structure while loosening their rules.

industries.industry: Securities broker-dealers and retail foreign-currency firms
industries.note: Broker-dealers gain new intermediary roles on derivatives facilities, but retail foreign-currency transactions offered to non-eligible participants are brought under CFTC jurisdiction — a consumer protection aimed at fraudulent 'bucket shop' forex dealers.
